title: Square up a leaning stack of cartons in place, without taking it apart
instruction: This stack could fall. Square it up by pushing, without taking it apart: in the end no carton may overhang the carton below it by more than 5 mm. Do not lift any carton off the one below it, and do not move the bottom carton more than 2 cm.
context: Cartons stacked out of line overhang the carton below and can fall on whoever works beside the stack. Unstacking and restacking would be easy; the task is the in-place correction a stockroom or warehouse worker makes with careful pushes, squaring a stack that is close to toppling without lifting any carton or knocking it over.
setup: World frame for this text: 'in front' is away from the arm bases, 'left' and 'right' are from the robot's view, heights are above the table top, and the midline is halfway between the two arm bases. Cartons (loose): three closed corrugated-cardboard cartons of the same size and look, 80 mm by 80 mm in plan and 60 mm tall, kraft brown; the bottom one holds heavier goods (1.0 kg in all), the other two weigh 200 g each. They are stacked upright with their sides square to the table's edges and all centred 10.0 cm left of the midline (6.0 to 14.0 cm). Bottom carton (0 to 60 mm high): centred 30.0 cm in front of the arm bases (26.0 to 34.0 cm). Middle carton (60 to 120 mm high), resting on the bottom one: shifted 18 mm toward the robot, centred 28.2 cm in front (24.2 to 32.2 cm). Top carton (120 to 180 mm high), resting on the middle one: shifted a further 30 mm toward the robot, centred 25.2 cm in front (21.2 to 29.2 cm), so it overhangs the bottom carton by 48 mm. The stack stands on its own as set. Nothing else is on the table.
scoring: Every limit below is inclusive (a value exactly at a limit passes). A carton's overhang is how far any corner of its footprint sticks out past a side of the top face of the carton below it, measured square to that side (a ruler on each side; a turned carton is judged by its corners). A joint is squared when that overhang is at most 5 mm; there are two joints, middle on bottom and top on middle. A carton's gap is how far its lowest bottom corner is above the top face of the carton below it (for the bottom carton, above the table), measured square to that face, so a stack that rocks as a whole keeps every gap near zero. The stack is intact when all three cartons are upright (each carton's 60 mm height within 3 degrees of vertical), at rest (moving less than 1 cm/s and turning less than 0.5 rad/s) and each gap is at most 1 mm. Judged over the whole trial: the trial scores 0, even if things are put back, if at any moment any carton's gap exceeds 5 mm (lifted off the carton below), any carton's lowest bottom corner rises more than 15 mm above the lowest it has been in the trial (for example a fallen carton picked up and restacked), or the bottom carton's centre, seen from above, is more than 20 mm from where it started. Rocking the stack without lifting a carton off the one below is allowed. Score 1.0: the stack is intact and both joints are squared, with none of the whole-trial violations. Score 0.5: the stack is intact and exactly one joint is squared, with none of the violations. Score 0 in every other case: no joint squared (as at the start), any carton fallen, off the stack, tipped, held above the carton below or still moving, or any whole-trial violation. The trial ends at 1.0 once the 1.0 condition has held for 1 s; otherwise it scores the condition at the last step. The whole-trial record is cleared only when the scene is reset to the starting layout (every carton back within 0.5 mm of its start in one jump of more than 20 mm), not by rebuilding the start by hand.
reset_notes: Rebuild the stack on its tape marks with the 18 mm and 30 mm shifts toward the robot, sides square to the table's edges. Nothing is consumed; cartons that fall should be checked for crushed corners and replaced if deformed.
fidelity: Approximate. The cartons are rigid boxes of uniform density with the simulator's default friction, not measured cardboard friction; real cartons flex, have flaps and seams, and may be unevenly filled. The stack is set near its tipping limit (7 mm of margin at the bottom joint), so a real stack built to the same marks may be more or less stable. Carton faces are unmarked, so a carton turned about the vertical is judged only by its corners.
